newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - June M3 grows annualised 6.4 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - June M3 grows annualised 6.4 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from analysts on June M3 money supply, which was at an annualised rate of 6.4 percent compared with the 1996 fourth quarter.
The Bundesbank said M3 growth slowed markedly in June compared with the rise in May.
GERHARD GREBE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANK JULIUS BAER IN FRANKFURT
"These figures are naturally very good. The reduced lending and stronger monetary capital formation is very positive.

The slower credit expansion means the economy is not growing so strongly. I would say these figures show a normalisation of money supply growth. The figures should stay within the corridor. These figures show there is no reason for the Bundesbank to increase interest rates."
NICK STAMENKOVIC, ECONOMIST, DKB INTERNATIONAL, LONDON:

"I think they are a good set of figures. Looking at the breakdown, it is certainly bond market friendly. I think the key aspect was the slowdown we saw in private sector lending. That has been stuck fairly high recently... So that is the most encouraging aspect to the figures. In addition, we have seen a pickup in capital formation, which does suggest that German investors have found funds increasingly attractive in June. In combination, (these) two factors should help the bond market.

"I think the Bundesbank will be happy to leave monetary policy on hold for the moment. I think the deutschemark stabilised last week, helped by the Ifo last week. The markets are worried about a soft euro.

"I think it is very important to see money supply growth coming into the target range so that from this side we have further confirmation that the Bundesbank will not change short-term rates in the foreseeable future.

"We think M3 growth will be at least at the upper end of the range for the rest of the year because, even with the change, the underlying trends in money capital formation on one the one hand and bank lending are still in favour in growth of money supply of about 6.5 percent and therefore I think the growth will not come down much further.
"We hardly have evidence to believe that monetary capital formation will shrink significantly in the coming months on the basis of current levels of long-term interest rates.

"The underlying trend rate of money supply growth is certainly in the range of around the rate of 6.5 to seven percent, which is certainly in the range of 6.5 to 7 percent and is somewhat too high in the medium-term when the Bundesbank says five percent is correct.
"I think M3 is a low-key variable for monetary policy decisions and I think the market is looking at other areas. In the short-term it is realistic that the dollar will rise above 1.80 marks.
